sections.overview: The Kentish Plover is a small shorebird of warm coasts, salt lagoons and saline flats across much of the Old World; newer bird lists also place it in Anarhynchus.
sections.identification: In breeding plumage the male has a black breast band interrupted at the front, dark facial marks and a rufous nape; the smaller-looking Little Ringed Plover (C. dubius) instead has a complete black chest band and conspicuous yellow eye-ring.
sections.habitat: It nests on open sandy beaches, dunes and salt-lagoon margins with sparse vegetation, where bare ground lets adults conceal eggs and chicks.
sections.diet: It feeds on small invertebrates, especially insects, but also crustaceans, molluscs, worms and spiders gathered on exposed shores and saline wetlands.
sections.behavior: Some populations are resident while others migrate short or long distances; in France many birds move south after gathering from midsummer into autumn.
sections.reproduction: The pair lays eggs in a shallow scrape on bare sand or salt-flat substrate, and one parent—often the male—may raise the precocial chicks after incubation.
sections.ecology: It is the coastal, saline-habitat counterpart to the mostly inland Little Ringed Plover in the neighbouring fiche; both rely on open ground but their breeding landscapes and collar patterns differ.
sections.conservation: The global Red List category is Least Concern, but the French breeding population is assessed as Vulnerable and faces disturbance from beach recreation and loss of nesting habitat.
